messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Thanh Nguyen is a 46-year-old Vietnamese-American firefighter who presented for psychological evaluation following a period of escalating distress that he described, with visible difficulty, as "things finally getting too loud to ignore." Divorced for three years and living alone in a modest apartment near his fire station, Thanh carries himself with the composed bearing of someone who has spent decades managing other people's emergencies. What brought him to the clinic, however, was something that happened not in a burning building but in a humanitarian deployment he undertook eight years ago, a two-month stint as a relief worker in a conflict zone in Southeast Asia where his firefighting and emergency medical skills were considered assets. It is from those eight weeks that the current clinical picture appears to originate.

Thanh had volunteered with a small international relief organization, and within days of arriving he was working in field conditions for which nothing had prepared him. He witnessed the aftermath of shelling — collapsed structures, fires set deliberately, people pulled from rubble — and was present during an attack on a distribution site in which an explosion occurred close enough to knock him from his feet. In the chaos that followed, he encountered evidence of systematic sexual violence against women and girls in the camp, including survivors who disclosed what had been done to them while Thanh was among the few personnel present. He was asked to document injuries. He did so, but he has never been able to fully account for the sequence of those hours in his memory. The timeline fractures somewhere around the explosion, and what comes before and after it refuses to arrange itself into a coherent order. He knows things happened — he knows what he saw and what he was asked to do — but when he tries to speak about it, the words dissolve. He has sat across from his former wife, from a station chaplain, from a close colleague, and each time arrived at the same wall: the knowledge present, the language absent.

In the years since returning, Thanh's world has quietly contracted. At the fire station, he functions capably on calls, but the environment carries its own hazards. During a training exercise eighteen months ago, a controlled detonation used to simulate a structural collapse sent him to his knees in the parking lot, heart hammering, certain for several seconds that he was back in the camp. He has since positioned himself during drills so that he is never near the demonstration charges, a small tactical adjustment his colleagues have not questioned. More disruptive is what happens in the station's quieter moments — the long overnight silences between calls. Thanh finds those stretches almost unbearable. He has come to feel that stillness is not rest but warning, that something terrible is accumulating in the quiet, and he has developed a habit of moving through the dormitory, checking on colleagues, manufacturing small sounds, in order to break the silence before it can mean something.

Off duty, he has found himself increasingly reactive in ordinary social situations. When he witnessed a man verbally intimidating a woman at a gas station, he intervened with a force that alarmed him afterward — not because the intervention was wrong, but because the rage that accompanied it felt disproportionate and not entirely his own. Comments overheard about sexual violence, even in news broadcasts or casual conversation, produce a visceral response he struggles to contain. He had come to believe that these reactions confirmed something he feared: that the person who came home from that deployment was not the same person who left, and that the original Thanh — the one who had clear values, a marriage, a sense of where he belonged — had been permanently displaced. He acted in ways over there, or failed to act in ways, that he cannot reconcile with who he understood himself to be. He does not elaborate on the specifics, but the shame is evident.

To manage the intrusive material, Thanh has developed rituals — specific sequences of thought he runs through before sleep and before certain situations, a private logic he believes may prevent further harm. When the feelings become too large, he has, on several occasions, hurt himself physically, pressing or striking his own body, and he reports this with the matter-of-fact tone of someone describing a pressure valve. The physical pain, he says, is at least a pain he understands.

What finally brought him to seek help was his teenage son's recent visit, during which Thanh recognized that he had nothing to offer the boy — no ease, no presence, no sense that his own life had a shape worth inhabiting. He is most afraid, he said at intake, that it is already too late to find out whether it does.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Memory: Pain Recall — the vignette does not describe Thanh experiencing physical pain in the same bodily locations as during the traumatic event when the memory returns: Pain Recall (Memory): Thanh's self-harm is described as deliberately inflicting physical pain to release overwhelming feelings, and the vignette notes physical pain he 'understands.' However, the specific symptom — re-experiencing physical pain in the same body parts as during the traumatic event when the memory returns — is never described. These are clinically distinct phenomena and the latter is absent.
- Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed — while the vignette conveys loss and contraction, it does not explicitly reflect the belief that his life has been destroyed by the trauma: Life Destroyed (Negative Appraisals): The vignette conveys that Thanh's world has 'quietly contracted,' his marriage ended, and he feels he has 'nothing to offer.' However, the core belief that the trauma has destroyed his life is not explicitly or clearly paraphrased. The closing reflection gestures toward it but remains ambiguous.
- Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere — the vignette references loss of his original sense of self and displacement, but does not explicitly capture the feeling that he no longer belongs anywhere: Belong Nowhere (Negative Appraisals): The vignette states the 'original Thanh' was 'permanently displaced' and that he lost his marriage and sense of self, but the specific appraisal of no longer belonging anywhere — a sense of social/existential rootlessness — is not clearly illustrated or paraphrased in the vignette.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Thanh Nguyen is a 46-year-old Vietnamese-American firefighter who presented for psychological evaluation following a period of escalating distress that he described, with visible difficulty, as "things finally getting too loud to ignore." Divorced for three years and living alone in a modest apartment near his fire station, Thanh carries himself with the composed bearing of someone who has spent decades managing other people's emergencies. What brought him to the clinic, however, was something that happened not in a burning building but in a humanitarian deployment he undertook eight years ago, a two-month stint as a relief worker in a conflict zone in Southeast Asia where his firefighting and emergency medical skills were considered assets. It is from those eight weeks that the current clinical picture appears to originate.

Thanh had volunteered with a small international relief organization, and within days of arriving he was working in field conditions for which nothing had prepared him. He witnessed the aftermath of shelling — collapsed structures, fires set deliberately, people pulled from rubble — and was present during an attack on a distribution site in which an explosion occurred close enough to knock him from his feet. The blast threw him hard against a concrete barrier; his left shoulder and the side of his head took the impact. In the chaos that followed, he encountered evidence of systematic sexual violence against women and girls in the camp, including survivors who disclosed what had been done to them while Thanh was among the few personnel present. He was asked to document injuries. He did so, but he has never been able to fully account for the sequence of those hours in his memory. The timeline fractures somewhere around the explosion, and what comes before and after it refuses to arrange itself into a coherent order. He knows things happened — he knows what he saw and what he was asked to do — but when he tries to speak about it, the words dissolve. He has sat across from his former wife, from a station chaplain, from a close colleague, and each time arrived at the same wall: the knowledge present, the language absent.

In the years since returning, Thanh's world has quietly contracted. At the fire station, he functions capably on calls, but the environment carries its own hazards. During a training exercise eighteen months ago, a controlled detonation used to simulate a structural collapse sent him to his knees in the parking lot, heart hammering, certain for several seconds that he was back in the camp. In those moments, a dull, pressured ache rises in his left shoulder and along the left side of his head — the same places that absorbed the impact of the blast — as though the memory carries its own bodily record, insisting on being felt in the precise locations where it first registered. He has since positioned himself during drills so that he is never near the demonstration charges, a small tactical adjustment his colleagues have not questioned. More disruptive is what happens in the station's quieter moments — the long overnight silences between calls. Thanh finds those stretches almost unbearable. He has come to feel that stillness is not rest but warning, that something terrible is accumulating in the quiet, and he has developed a habit of moving through the dormitory, checking on colleagues, manufacturing small sounds, in order to break the silence before it can mean something.

Off duty, he has found himself increasingly reactive in ordinary social situations. When he witnessed a man verbally intimidating a woman at a gas station, he intervened with a force that alarmed him afterward — not because the intervention was wrong, but because the rage that accompanied it felt disproportionate and not entirely his own. Comments overheard about sexual violence, even in news broadcasts or casual conversation, produce a visceral response he struggles to contain. He had come to believe that these reactions confirmed something he feared: that the person who came home from that deployment was not the same person who left, and that the original Thanh — the one who had clear values, a marriage, a sense of where he belonged — had been permanently displaced. What frightened him most was the accompanying conviction that the trauma had not merely changed his life but had demolished it entirely, that the structure of everything he had built — his marriage, his sense of vocation, his place in his own family — was rubble as surely as anything he had pulled people from overseas. He did not feel that he had lost his footing; he felt there was no ground left to stand on. His Vietnamese family gathered on weekends in his parents' home across town, and he had stopped going. His colleagues shared meals and easy conversation in the station kitchen, and he sat outside it. He was certain, in a way that felt less like depression than like clear-eyed assessment, that he no longer belonged anywhere — not to the culture he had grown up in, not to the profession he had chosen, not to the family he had started and then lost. He acted in ways over there, or failed to act in ways, that he cannot reconcile with who he understood himself to be. He does not elaborate on the specifics, but the shame is evident.

To manage the intrusive material, Thanh has developed rituals — specific sequences of thought he runs through before sleep and before certain situations, a private logic he believes may prevent further harm. When the feelings become too large, he has, on several occasions, hurt himself physically, pressing or striking his own body, and he reports this with the matter-of-fact tone of someone describing a pressure valve. The physical pain, he says, is at least a pain he understands. What finally brought him to seek help was his teenage son's recent visit, during which Thanh recognized that he had nothing to offer the boy — no ease, no presence, no sense that his own life had a shape worth inhabiting. He is most afraid, he said at intake, that it is already too late to find out whether it does.
